questions.prompt: You tuned PPO learning rate and reward weights by looking at success on evaluation seeds 1000-1099, then report the best result on those same seeds. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong: with 100 episodes per seed the sample is large enough to remove any bias from tuning.
The learning rate should have been tuned on the nominal split rather than on the perturbed split.
The evaluation seeds were used for tuning, so the number is optimistic; tune elsewhere and freeze first.
The seeds should be negative integers to avoid overlap with the simulator seed.
questions.explanation: Choices made after seeing evaluation results make evaluation part of training. The number is biased upward, whatever the sample size.

questions.prompt: 27 successes in 30 held-out episodes. Lower end of the 95 % Wilson interval (3 decimals).
questions.explanation: Wilson: [0.744, 0.965]. The lower bound is below 0.80.

questions.prompt: Two runs of train_ppo.py with the same seed give different evaluation returns on CPU. Which first step is most likely to fix it?
options: Use a larger batch size and fewer epochs per update so that the averaging removes the noise.
Set torch to one thread and seed python, numpy, torch and the environment.
Switch to a GPU, which is deterministic by default.
Lower the learning rate until the runs agree.
questions.explanation: Multi-threaded reductions and unseeded components are the usual causes. Fix determinism first; do not hide it with hyperparameters.

questions.prompt: A behaviour-cloning policy has a very low held-out action MSE but fails often in closed loop. What is the best explanation?
options: The MSE must have been computed on the training demos.
The network is far too large for 500 demonstrations and only needs more weight decay to fix it.
Closed-loop success can never be predicted from any offline number, so offline MSE is useless.
Small errors push the policy into states the demonstrations never visited, and they compound.
questions.explanation: Covariate shift: the policy is evaluated on its own state distribution, not the expert's.

questions.prompt: Training runs at 300 environment steps per second. How many hours do 1.8 M steps take? (3 decimals)
questions.explanation: 1.8e6 / 300 = 6000 s = 1.667 h, close to the 2 h limit.

questions.prompt: Write the reward for the reach-and-grasp primitive: list the terms, say what each one is for, and name one way a policy could exploit your design (reward hacking) plus how you would detect it.
rubric: Lists a dense distance term, one-off grasp/lift bonuses, an action penalty and a time penalty with a reason for each.
Names a concrete exploit (for example hovering near the object, or lifting without holding) tied to the chosen terms.
Gives a detection method: watch episodes, log the terms separately, check success against return.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: Domain randomisation for training uses mass +-5 % and no action delay, but the real robot and the held-out test have +-30 % mass and 40 ms delay. What do you expect?
options: The policy will be robust everywhere because training was clean, stable and easy.
Little robustness: the test lies outside the training distribution, so success may drop sharply.
Exactly the same success as on the nominal simulator, since training converged.
The policy will fail to train at all.
questions.explanation: A policy is only robust over what it saw. Narrow ranges mean extrapolation at test time.
